evidence: a hidden powershell.exe process opened a raw TCP socket to 203.0.113.50 on port 4444
the same script fell back to port 8888 on 198.51.100.77
the operator ran cmd.exe to launch a netcat-style relay, which also connected to 203.0.113.50 on port 4444
cases.report_text: Intrusion summary, week 41. The operator gained a reverse shell on the finance file server when a hidden powershell.exe process opened a raw TCP socket to 203.0.113.50 on port 4444. After the perimeter proxy began resetting that connection, the same script fell back to port 8888 on 198.51.100.77. Later the operator ran cmd.exe to launch a netcat-style relay, which also connected to 203.0.113.50 on port 4444. None of these ports is used by a sanctioned application, and ordinary shell processes in this network make outbound connections only to ports 80 and 443. We assess that the operator chose arbitrary high ports to avoid the web-proxy allow list. Defenders should alert on command shells that open outbound sessions to these two ports.

evidence: The operator staged plink.exe on the pivot host and used it to build a reverse SSH tunnel to the staging server at 203.0.113.88 on port 2222
the built-in ssh.exe client was used for the same purpose, this time to port 8022 on 198.51.100.145
administrators legitimately reach only the bastion host at 192.0.2.10, which listens on port 2222
cases.report_text: The operator staged plink.exe on the pivot host and used it to build a reverse SSH tunnel to the staging server at 203.0.113.88 on port 2222, forwarding RDP back into the victim network. On a second host the built-in ssh.exe client was used for the same purpose, this time to port 8022 on 198.51.100.145 after the first staging server was taken down. Our SSH inventory shows that administrators legitimately reach only the bastion host at 192.0.2.10, which listens on port 2222; every other destination on ports 2222 or 8022 is unsanctioned. Neither tunnel used a standard SSH port, which allowed them to slip past a firewall rule that only inspected port 22. Defenders should alert on SSH clients reaching those ports, excluding the bastion host.

evidence: the loader ran as a DLL through rundll32.exe, which then opened an outbound TLS session to 203.0.113.141 on port 8443
A parallel infection chain used regsvr32.exe to load a remote scriptlet and later beaconed to 198.51.100.9 on port 9001
cases.report_text: In the second wave the loader ran as a DLL through rundll32.exe, which then opened an outbound TLS session to 203.0.113.141 on port 8443. A parallel infection chain used regsvr32.exe to load a remote scriptlet and later beaconed to 198.51.100.9 on port 9001. Neither Windows binary has any reason to talk to the internet in this environment, and in our telemetry they have never connected to any destination on ports 8443 or 9001. Browsers do use port 8443 for some internal management consoles, so the detection should key on the two binaries together with the port rather than on the port alone. Analysts should treat any such connection from these binaries as hands-on-keyboard command-and-control activity.

evidence: The two observed so far, 198.51.100.23 and 198.51.100.24, sit in the same 198.51.100.0/24 block, and the operator reached them on ports 8080 and 8000

cases.report_text: The loader family stages modules from a small group of rented servers. The two observed so far, 198.51.100.23 and 198.51.100.24, sit in the same 198.51.100.0/24 block, and the operator reached them on ports 8080 and 8000 using a dropped binary and PowerShell. Our review found no sanctioned business process that connects to that block on these ports, with one exception: browsers such as chrome.exe and msedge.exe reach the provider's customer portal in the same block on port 8080 and must be excluded from any detection. Because the infrastructure is rented in bulk, further addresses in the block are likely to be used, so the rule should cover the whole prefix instead of the two known hosts.

evidence: The implant locates its controller by resolving hostnames under cloud-sync-assist.example roughly once a minute
using api.cloud-sync-assist.example for tasking and cdn.cloud-sync-assist.example for staged modules
In the first infection the lookups came from rundll32.exe, loaded from a scheduled task; in the second they came from powershell.exe running a hidden loop
cases.report_text: The implant locates its controller by resolving hostnames under cloud-sync-assist.example roughly once a minute, using api.cloud-sync-assist.example for tasking and cdn.cloud-sync-assist.example for staged modules. In the first infection the lookups came from rundll32.exe, loaded from a scheduled task; in the second they came from powershell.exe running a hidden loop. The domain was registered three days before first use and has no connection to any vendor in our supply chain, so any lookup of it is suspicious. Because attackers can change the subdomains at will, defenders should match on the parent domain and on the two host processes observed rather than on the individual hostnames.

evidence: Each beacon looks up a name whose first label is a lowercase hexadecimal string of 20 or more characters under the zone relay-hub.example
for example 9f2a61c0d4e87b35a1c2e7.relay-hub.example
cases.report_text: The backdoor tunnels its tasking through DNS. Each beacon looks up a name whose first label is a lowercase hexadecimal string of 20 or more characters under the zone relay-hub.example, for example 9f2a61c0d4e87b35a1c2e7.relay-hub.example. The zone is shared hosting, and legitimate customers use short human-readable names such as status.relay-hub.example or build identifiers of about twelve characters. In the incident the lookups came from rundll32.exe and from a dropped binary in the Public profile, at roughly one query per forty seconds. Hexadecimal labels of this length carry encoded command data and are not produced by any browser.

evidence: In one session curl.exe resolved ip-echo.example, and in another a powershell.exe one-liner using Invoke-RestMethod resolved the fallback service myaddr.test
cases.report_text: Before configuring its tunnel, the operator checked the victim's external address from an interactive shell. In one session curl.exe resolved ip-echo.example, and in another a powershell.exe one-liner using Invoke-RestMethod resolved the fallback service myaddr.test. This lookup is a recognisable step in hands-on-keyboard discovery because no business application on the finance subnet relies on either service. Ordinary users do sometimes open the same address-check page in a web browser, so only command-line clients should be flagged. The behaviour precedes tunnel creation by a few minutes and gives defenders an early chance to intervene.

evidence: The dropper wrote its second stage to C:\Users\ana\AppData\Local\Temp\wsupd.exe and executed it directly from there
That process resolved hosts under dyn-host.example, a free dynamic DNS service, for example node7.dyn-host.example, to find its controller
cases.report_text: The dropper wrote its second stage to C:\Users\ana\AppData\Local\Temp\wsupd.exe and executed it directly from there. That process resolved hosts under dyn-host.example, a free dynamic DNS service, for example node7.dyn-host.example, to find its controller, and it kept changing the host label when a name was blocked. No sanctioned application here uses dynamic DNS, and no executable running from a user Temp directory should be performing such lookups. Browsers may reach dynamic DNS names for personal use, so the signal depends on the process running from the Temp directory and not on the domain alone.

lookalike.cmd: schtasks /create /tn OneDriveStartup /tr C:\Program Files\Microsoft OneDrive\OneDrive.exe /sc onlogon

evidence: The operator ran schtasks.exe /create /tn SyncHelper /tr C:\Users\Public\Libraries\sync.exe /sc onlogon /ru SYSTEM
the same pattern appeared with the binary stored under C:\Users\bob\AppData\Roaming\Zoom\
cases.report_text: Persistence on the compromised workstation was established with a scheduled task created during a hands-on-keyboard session. The operator ran schtasks.exe /create /tn SyncHelper /tr C:\Users\Public\Libraries\sync.exe /sc onlogon /ru SYSTEM, so the payload would start at every logon with elevated rights. On a second host the same pattern appeared with the binary stored under C:\Users\bob\AppData\Roaming\Zoom\. Routine schtasks.exe use in this environment is limited to querying tasks, for example schtasks /query /fo LIST, and administrators schedule their own jobs from C:\Scripts. Task creation that runs at logon from a user-writable folder has not been seen from administrators.

lookalike.cmd: powershell.exe -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -Command $a=New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute C:\Program Files\Contoso\agent.exe; Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName AgentRefresh -Action $a -Trigger (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn)

evidence: The operator started powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden, shortened to -w hidden in the later builds
the one-liner called New-ScheduledTaskAction and then Register-ScheduledTask with a logon trigger
our endpoint management client launched by ccmexec.exe registers tasks in this way during software deployment and must be excluded
cases.report_text: The second-stage script persisted by registering a scheduled task straight from a hidden PowerShell session. The operator started powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden, shortened to -w hidden in the later builds, and the one-liner called New-ScheduledTaskAction and then Register-ScheduledTask with a logon trigger so that a payload under the Public profile ran at every sign-in. Legitimate use of these cmdlets exists: our endpoint management client launched by ccmexec.exe registers tasks in this way during software deployment and must be excluded. All other registrations from a hidden PowerShell window should be reviewed. Scripts that run hidden without registering a task, such as the nightly backup, are common and not in scope.

evidence: They ran nltest.exe /dclist:corp.example to list domain controllers, nltest /domain_trusts to map trust relationships, and nltest /dsgetdc:corp.example to identify the nearest controller
cases.report_text: Within ten minutes of landing, the operator began enumerating the domain from an interactive cmd.exe session. They ran nltest.exe /dclist:corp.example to list domain controllers, nltest /domain_trusts to map trust relationships, and nltest /dsgetdc:corp.example to identify the nearest controller. The commands were typed by hand and spaced a few seconds apart, which indicates a person rather than an automated tool. Domain controller discovery is a typical precursor to lateral movement. Our baseline shows nltest.exe is almost never run on workstations, and when help-desk staff do use it they run secure channel checks such as nltest /sc_query, which are not discovery of other hosts.

positive.cmd: cmd.exe /c systeminfo & whoami /all & netstat -ano & arp -a > C:\Users\Public\o.txt

evidence: the operator pasted a single chained command into cmd.exe rather than running each tool on its own: cmd.exe /c systeminfo & whoami /all & netstat -ano & arp -a
a chain that combines systeminfo, whoami /all and netstat -ano in one command line is not seen in routine activity
cases.report_text: To profile each new host, the operator pasted a single chained command into cmd.exe rather than running each tool on its own: cmd.exe /c systeminfo & whoami /all & netstat -ano & arp -a > C:\Users\Public\o.txt. The output file was collected a few minutes later. Individually these tools are common in administration, and our baseline contains many single runs of whoami and ipconfig, but a chain that combines systeminfo, whoami /all and netstat -ano in one command line is not seen in routine activity. Some operators type netstat /ano with a slash instead of a dash, so the detection should accept both spellings.

No baseline cmd.exe line contains all three (0 of 400).
